stem: A50-year-old man who smokes 20 cigarettes per day and works as a plumber presents to the General Practitioner for review. His blood pressure is 132/82 mmHg, heart rate is 75 bpm and regular. There is quiet wheeze on auscultation of the chest. His body mass index is 27 kg/m. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin(Hb) 138 g/l 135-175 g/l White cell count(WCC) 7.2×10/L 4-11×10/L Platelets(PLT) 201×10/L 150-400×10/L Sodium(Na+) 141 mmol/l 135-145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 4.3 mmol/L 3.5-5.0 mmol/L Creatinine (Cr) 90 μmol/L 50-120 μmol/L Forced vital capacity(FVC) 88% of predicted Forced expiratory volume in 1s 70% of predicted (FEV)/FVC pre-bronchodilator FEV/FVC post-bronchodilator 72% of predicted Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: This patient has a significant smoking history and an obstructive picture on lung function testing with no reversibility on bronchodilator testing. In asthma, an improvement in FEVgreater than 12% would be expected after salbutamol. Standard therapy for chronic obstructive pulmonary disease where there is no significant reversible component usually involves an inhaled long-acting muscarinic antagonist. High-dose inhaled corticosteroids and an inhaled long-acting beta-agonist can be added in to improve symptom control. Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease Media explanations.

stem: A52-year-old who has been diagnosed with alcoholism is admitted to the Emergency Department with a fever, confusion and abdominal distension. According to his partner, he has been unwell for the past 48 hours. His temperature is 38.2°℃, blood pressure is 90/50 mmHg and heart rate is 100 bpm and regular. The abdomen is distended with marked tenderness on palpation and evidence of large volume ascites. There is pitting oedema of both lower limbs. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin(Hb) 101 g/l 135-175 g/l White cell count(WCC) 15.2×10/L 4-11×109/L Platelets(PLT) 55×10/L 150-400×10/L Sodium(Na+) 132 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/L Potassium(K+) 4.8 mmol/L 3.5-5.0 mmol/L Creatinine(Cr) 67 μmol/L 50-120 μmol/L Which of the following is the most appropriate antibiotic choice in this case?
explanation: The clinical picture here fits with a diagnosis of spontaneous bacterial peritonitis with evidence of chronic liver disease, tense ascites and pyrexia. A third-generation cephalosporin such as cefotaxime is the initial intervention of choice because it has broad-spectrum activity against Gram-negative bacteria. Escherichia coli and Klebsiella pneumoniae are common causes of spontaneous bacterial peritonitis. In patients with renal impairment, mortality from spontaneous bacterial peritonitis may be as high as 67%. Peritonitis and SBP explanations.

stem: A 29-year-old woman presents to the Outpatient Department for review. She has a malignant melanoma on her leg, prior to progression to surgical excision. She is a smoker of 10 cigarettes per day and her body mass index(BMI) is elevated at 29 kg/m. The lesion is 8 mm in diameter. What has the biggest negative impact on her prognosis?
options: Position of the lesion on her leg
explanation: The thickness of the lesion is closely associated with outcomes from melanoma and it drives the T score. · T0: no evidence of primary tumour · Tis: tumour in situ Q. Answered Flagged · T1:thickness 1mm or less (a) without ulceration and mitosis1/mm2;(b) with ulceration or mitoses =1/mm2 · T2: thickness 1.01-2.00 mm(a) without ulceration; (b) with ulceration · T3: thickness 2.01-4.00 mm(a) without ulceration; (b) with ulceration · T4:thickness4.00 mm (a) without ulceration;(b) with ulceration. For melanomas 1.0-4.0 mm in Breslow thickness, the risk of metastatic spread to regional lymph nodes is 15-25%. This rises with increasing tumour thickness. For thick melanomas which are4.0 mm in Breslow thickness, lymph node positivity rates are 25-40%. Malignant Melanoma Media explanations.

stem: A57-year-old man presents to the Renal Clinic with poorly controlled hypertension and New York Heart Association class Il heart failure. He has failed a trial of ramipril due to an elevation in serum creatinine. His blood pressure is 150/90 mmHg, heart rate is 74 bpm and regular. His abdomen is soft and non-tender and his body mass index is 25 kg/m. Investigations: Which of the following is the most useful investigation? Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin(Hb) 121 g/l 135-175 g/L White cell count(WCC) 6.2×10/L 4-11×10/L Platelets (PLT) 209×10/ 150-400×10/L Sodium(Na+) 142 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/L Potassium (K+) 4.9 mmol/L 3.5-5.0 mmol/L Rose to 5.3 mmol/l after seven days of 2.5 mg ramipril Creatinine (Cr) 110 μmol/L 50-120 μmol/l Rose to 152 μmol/l after seven days of 2.5 mg ramipril
explanation: The electrolyte changes seen here raise the possibility of renal artery stenosis, which may be unilateral or bilateral, driving the rise in creatinine seen after angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE)-inhibitor initiation. It is a rise above 30% which raises significant concern and according to National Institute for Health and Care Excellence guidelines should prompt a hunt for an underlying cause. A renal CT angiogram is the logical next step, which may confirm a significant renal artery stenosis. Renal Artery Stenosis explanations.

stem: A 19-year-old man presents to the Rheumatology Clinic with chronic lower back pain and stiffness which is so severe for the first two hours each morning that he finds it impossible to get up on time. He has tried ibuprofen and obtained a naproxen prescription from his General Practitioner, but this is making little difference to his symptoms. The pain improves during the day, with more activity. He has had two episodes of uveitis in the past year but is otherwise well. Examination reveals that forward and lateral flexion are both limited by pain and stiffness. nvestigations: Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin(Hb) 142 g/l 135-175 g/l White cell count (WCC) 8.1×10/L 4-11×10/L Platelets(PLT) 291×10/L 150-400×10/L Sodium(Na+) 143 mmol/l 135-145 mmol/L Potassium (K+) 4.5 mmol/L 3.5-5.0 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 92 μmol/L 50-120 μmol/L C-reactive protein (CRP) 52 mg/l 10 mg/l Which of the following is the most likely underlying diagnosis?
explanation: This patient's symptoms of lower back pain and stiffness, particularly for the first two hours each morning are consistent with a diagnosis of ankylosing spondylitis. Other features alongside back pain can include uveitis, psoriasis and inflammatory bowel disease. Plain X-ray may demonstrate blurring of the sacroiliac joint in keeping with inflammation, although magnetic resonance imaging may be needed to confirm disease activity. Ankylosing spondylitis is one condition where intervention with tumour necrosis factor modulators is indicated at an early stage. According to National Institute for Health and Care Excellence guidelines they may be introduced after two different non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs have failed to control symptoms. Ankylosing Spondylitis Media explanations.

stem: A 27-year-old woman who is 34 weeks' pregnant is admitted to the Emergency Department with hypertension, epigastric pain and proteinuria. She has worsening bruising and bleeding around her gums, which has developed over the past 24 hours. Her blood pressure is 155/90 mmHg and her heart rate is 95 bpm and regular. She has extensive bruising over both her arms and legs. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin(Hb) 92 g/l 115-155 g/l White cell count (WCC) 12.1×10/L 4-11×10/L Platelets (PLT) 55×10/L 150-400×10/L International normalised ratio(INR) Sodium (Na+) 142 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/L Potassium (K+) 4.7 mmol/L 3.5-5.0 mmol/L Creatinine (Cr) 85 μmol/L 50-120 μmol/l Alanine transaminase (ALT) 271 U/L 1-40 U/L Urine Protein ++ Which of the following is the most useful next intervention?
explanation: This patient has haemolysis, elevated liver enzymes and low platelets syndrome, with features of pre- eclampsia. In this situation, magnesium is recommended by National Institute for Health and Care Excellence guidelines. A usual loading dose of 4g magnesium sulphate is given over ten minutes, followed by 1 g/hr as a maintenance dose. It is proven to reduce the risk of seizures in this situation and helps to buy time for controlling blood pressure and achieving haemostasis before moving to delivery of the fetus. HELLP Syndrome Q explanations.

stem: An 18-year-old woman presents to the Haematology Clinic for review. She has regular menses every month which have always been heavy. On examination, she reveals that her father has to take care because he bleeds after tooth extraction. Physical examination is unremarkable. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin (Hb) 104 g/l 115-155 g/l White cell count (WCC) 6.7×10/L 4-11×109/L Platelets(PLT) 191×10/L 150-400×10/L Sodium(Na+) 143 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/L Potassium (K+) 4.5 mmol/L 3.5-5.0 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 90 μmol/L 50-120 μmol/L Prothrombin time 12.3 s 11-13.5 s Activated partial thromboplastin time 26 s 23-30 s (APTT) Which of the following is the most likely cause of the patient's menorrhagia?
explanation: Von Willebrand's disease is caused by a deficiency of von Willebrand's factor.60-80% of cases are type 1, which is inherited, as here,in an autosomal-dominant pattern and causes relatively mild bleeding symptoms, such as menorrhagia or bleeding after tooth extraction. Between 19% and 45% of the enzyme is present. Both tranexamic acid and desmopressin are potential interventions to reduce bleeding for patients undergoing surgery. Disseminated Intravascular Coagulation Media explanations.

stem: A 54-year-old smoker presents to the Oncology Ward with a 3-month history of epigastric pain radiating to her back. She has lost 5 kg in weight and is finding it very difficult to eat. Her abdomen is soft, although she has some tenderness in the epigastrium. Her body mass index(BMI) is 23 kg/m. Investigations Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin (Hb) 100 g/l 115-155 g/L White cell count (WCC) 9.1×109/L 4-11×10/L Platelets(PLT) 152×10/L 150-400×10/L Sodium(Na+) 142 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/L Potassium(K+) 3.7 mmol/L 3.5-5.0 mmol/L Creatinine (Cr) 90 μmol/L 50-120 μmol/L Ultrasound abdomen Mass in the head of the pancreas What tumour marker is most likely to be elevated?
explanation: Cancer antigen 19-9 is a tetrasaccharide found on the surface of cells. It plays an important role in the cell- to-cell recognition process. It is produced by exocrine pancreatic carcinoma cells. Although it is not used in the diagnosis of pancreatic cancer, Cancer antigen 19-9 can be used to monitor for recurrence of cancer post pancreatectomy or after a period chemotherapy. Pancreatic cancer Media explanations.

stem: A 45-year-old Japanese woman presents to the Emergency Department with chest pain suggestive of angina. She has been feeling unwell for some weeks with headaches, blurred vision, gradual weight loss, fevers and joint pains. She is a non-smoker who takes no regular medication. Her blood pressure is 151/95 mmHg in the right arm, 135/82 mmHg in the left arm. She has a left carotid bruit. Fundoscopy reveals evidence of retinal venous congestion. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin(Hb) 101 g/l 115-155 g/l White cell count(WCC) 10.9×10/L 4-11×10/L Platelets(PLT) 301×10/L 150-400×10/L Sodium(Na+) 141 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/L Potassium(K+) 4.2 mmol/L 3.5-5.0 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 131 μmol/L 50-120 μmol/L Erythrocyte sedimentation rate(ESR) 102 mm/h 10 mm/h Electrocardiogram(ECG) Inferolateral ST depression Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: This patient is of Japanese ethnic origin and has symptoms of a vasculitis which appears to be affecting branches of the aorta(coronary arteries and the left carotid, at least). This is consistent with a diagnosis of Takayasu's arteritis, which is associated with the B52 human leukocyte antigen type. The retinal congestion seen on fundoscopy and the differential blood pressure between the arms are features to support the diagnosis. Both computed tomography angiography and magnetic resonance imaging can play a role in confirming the diagnosis. Most patients respond to high-dose corticosteroids and conventional disease- modifying agents such as azathioprine and cyclophosphamide may be used in combination. Anti-platelet agents can reduce the incidence of ischaemic cardiovascular events. Takayasu Arteritis explanations.

stem: A74-year-old man presents to the Outpatient Department with his wife. Over the past three months he has suffered from increasing short-term memory loss, falls and incontinence of urine on 2-3 occasions. His blood pressure is 148/85 mmHg and heart rate is 72 bpm and regular. He has no papilloedema. He is asked to walk across the room and it is noted that he has a broad-based shuffling gait. Routine bloods are unremarkable. Which of the following is the most likely cause of the patient's symptoms?
explanation: This patient has three main symptoms: short-term memory loss; incontinence of urine; and gait disturbance. Taken together with papilloedema, the possibility of normal-pressure hydrocephalus is raised. Magnetic resonance imaging may show ventricular enlargement out of proportion to the level of sulcal atrophy seen and periventricular lucency. Cerebrospinal fluid(CSF) pressure is normal or mildly elevated and initial treatment options include acetazolamide and larger volume lumbar puncture. Over the longer-term,a CSF shunt is usually required. Q.

stem: A54-year-old woman with non-alcoholic steatohepatitis and type Il diabetes presents to the General Practitioner for her 6-month follow up appointment following initiation of metformin 1g twice daily. She has improved her glucose control, lost 2 kg in weight and her transaminases have fallen. Which of the following is the primary mode of action of metformin?
options: Increases glucose excretion in the urine
explanation: Metformin is proven to reduce hepatic insulin resistance, which manifests as reduced hepatic glucose output. It is thought to act as an indirect adenosine monophosphate(AMP)-kinase activator and leads to increased excretion of bile acids into the faeces, which explains why some patients suffer from diarrhoea when the dose is up-titrated too quickly. It leads to modest weight loss, does not cause hypoglycaemia and has been shown to reduce cardiovascular events in patients with type ll diabetes mellitus. This makes it the default first choice for treatment of type ll diabetes mellitus. Q.

stem: A 59-year-old woman who has been diagnosed with obesity and type ll diabetes presents to the Dermatology Department with an ulcer over the medial malleolus. She says it has been there for many months and has slowly grown. The ulcer is around 2 cm in diameter and there is considerable slough and brown pigmentation around the ulcer. She has bilateral varicose veins. Which of the following is the most likely cause of the brown pigmentation seen here?
explanation: Increased venous pressure in the area surrounding a venous ulcer leads to extravasation of blood cells into the surrounding tissue. This results in deposition of haemosiderin, leading to a brown discoloration around the ulcer. Weight loss can help to reduce lower-limb venous pressure and three-layer compression bandaging can promote healing of the ulcer. A surgical solution to her varicose veins may also be possible and reduce the risk of further ulceration,although haemosiderin deposition does not reverse. Q.

stem: A 67-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department complaining of a problem with the vision out of his left eye. He also appears to have lost the ability to sweat on the left-hand side of the face. He has a 40- pack-year smoking history. There is a partial ptosis affecting the left eyelid and the pupil is constricted. Which of the following is the most useful next investigation?
explanation: This patient is a heavy smoker, which raises the possibility of a Pancoast's tumour affecting the apex of the lung. These tumours can involve the stellate ganglion (a component of the sympathetic nervous system) by local compression and this in turn leads to the development of Horner syndrome, with the features seen here of partial ptosis, pupil constriction and loss of sweating on the affected side. Q.

stem: A 29-year-old man has repeated attendance at the Emergency Department convinced that he has colon cancer. He has no symptoms of bowel disturbance and his father died of colon cancer at the age of 59. Physical examination is entirely normal and he has had a normal bloods screen. Nothing was found on colonoscopy some three months earlier. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: IlLness anxiety disorder (previously referred to as hypochondria) fits best with this patient's symptoms. He has a fixed belief that he has colon cancer despite normal findings on examination, blood testing and colonoscopy. The multiple presentations suggest this is illness anxiety disorder.In general, further invasive investigations should be avoided because they can actually drive further investigation-seeking behaviour. Patient education and reassurance are other important components of managing individuals with the disorder. Q.

stem: A52-year-old man is reviewed on the Medical Admissions Ward the morning after taking a paracetamol overdose. He has hypertension and well-controlled asthma and drinks four units of alcohol per week. He has recently lost his job and lives alone after splitting from his long term partner. Which of the following is the biggest risk factor for completed suicide in this case?
options: Paracetamol as the mode of self-harm
explanation: This patient has two significant reasons for social isolation, having lost his job and splitting up from his partner.In a man of any age, these two factors have the most significant impact on his risk of completed suicide. Other significant drivers, particularly in males, include impulsive behaviour, drug abuse and alcoholism (versus the very modest alcohol consumption seen here). Q.

stem: A57-year-old woman presents to the Outpatient Department for review. She reports shoulder pain and weakness mainly affecting her hips, shoulders and proximal leg muscles. She is vegetarian and admits to spending most of her time inside. Her blood pressure is 132/82mmHg,heart rate is 67 bpm and regular. She has 4/5 power weakness affecting her shoulders and hips, but no pain on palpation of the muscles. nvestigations: Which of the following is the most useful next investigation? Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin(Hb) 110 g/l 115-155 g/L White cell count (WCC) 7.2×10/L 4-11×10/L Platelets (PLT) 231×10/L 150-400×10/L Sodium(Na+) 143 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/L Potassium (K+) 4.5 mmol/l 3.5-5.0 mmol/l Creatinine(Cr) 95 μmol/L 50-120 μmol/l Phosphate(PO-) 0.6 mmol/L 0.8-1.5 mmol/l Calcium 2.1 mmol/l 2.1-2.65 mmol/l Alkaline phosphatase 289 U/L 30-130 U/L
explanation: This patient is a vegetarian who admits to staying inside, which raises the possibility of vitamin D deficiency. The proximal myopathy and blood picture with raised alkaline phosphatase, calcium borderline low and decreased phosphate fits with vitamin D deficiency and a secondary rise in PTH.25-hydroxy vitamin D is Likely to be significantly reduced. Vitamin D supplementation and encouraging greater sun exposure is likely to significantly improve her symptoms. Osteomalacia and rickets explanations.

stem: A 45-year-old woman presents to the Renal Clinic for review. She has palpitations,muscle weakness and bony pains which have worsened over the past few months. She has Sjogren syndrome and mild asthma and has had one episode of renal colic precipitating a presentation to the Emergency Department some two months earlier. Her blood pressure is 142/85 mmHg. nvestigations: Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin(Hb) 103 g/l 115-155 g/L White cell count (WCC) 7.9×10/L 4-11×10/L Platelets (PLT) 209×10/L 150-400×10/L Sodium(Na+) 143 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/L Potassium (K+) 3.2 mmol/l 3.5-5.0 mmol/l Bicarbonate(HCO) 16 mmol/L 23-29 mmol/l Chloride (Cl-) 115 mmol/L 98-106 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 149 μmol/l 50-120 μmol/l Calcium (Ca2+) 2.1 mmol/l 2.1-2.65 mmol/L Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: The clinical picture here with renal stones, low serum calcium and metabolic acidosis with hypokalaemia fits.

stem: A74-year-old retired plumber presents to the General Practitioner complaining of dull right-sided chest ache and shortness of breath which has steadily become worse over the last six months. He smokes five cigarettes per day. He has rheumatoid arthritis but this has burned out many years ago. He has reduced chest expansion on the right-hand side and it is dull to percussion at the right base with decreased breath sounds. Investigations: Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's pleural effusion? Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin(Hb) 129 g/l 135-175 g/L White cell count (WCC) 8.1×10/L 4-11×10/L Platelets (PLT) 189×10/L 150-400×10/L Sodium(Na+) 141 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 4.5 mmol/L 3.5-5.0 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 119 μmol/L 50-120 μmol/L Chest X-ray Large right-sided pleural effusion Bilateral pleural plaques
explanation: This patient has occupational exposure to asbestos through his previous role as a plumber and evidence of asbestos-related plaques on the chest X-ray. The duration of symptoms and the pleural effusion identified on chest X-ray is highly suggestive of a mesothelioma. Pleural biopsy under ultrasound or computed tomography guidance is the best way to confirm the diagnosis. Debulking surgery may improve quality of life and platinum-based chemotherapy has been proven to have a positive effect on symptoms. Mesothelioma and Other Asbestos Related Conditions Media explanations.

stem: A 24-year-old woman presents to the Outpatient Department complaining of recurrent nausea, a lack of appetite and recurrent hypoglycaemia over the past 3-4 weeks. She has type l diabetes and has progressively reduced her insulin because of hypos over the past 8 weeks. Her flash glucose monitor reveals glucose levels below 4.5mmol/l on a number of occasions during the day and 3-4 episodes of glucose below 2.8 mmol/L. Her blood pressure is 95/50 mmHg and her heart rate is 95 bpm and regular. Her body mass index is 21 kg/m. She looks tanned. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin (Hb) 99 g/l 115-155 g/L White cell count (WCC) 6.2×10/ 4-11×10/L Platelets(PLT) 272×10/L 150-400×10/L Sodium(Na+) 132 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/l Potassium(K+) 5.4 mmol/L 3.5-5.0 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 122μmol/L 50-120μmol/l Glucose (random) 5.4 mmol/l 11.1 mmol/l Which of the following is the most appropriate intervention?
explanation: Type I diabetes is associated with other autoimmune diseases, including autoimmune hypoadrenalism (Addison's disease), where the failure to produce adequate amounts of cortisol leads to hypotension, hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia and hypoglycaemia because of impaired storage of glycogen and an impaired counter-regulatory response. In this situation, starting hydrocortisone is imperative to prevent a worsening adrenal crisis and should be commenced ahead of a synacthen test if needed. After a first IV dose, it can be dosed twice a day orally, usually with a larger dose in the morning versus the evening. Doses of 100-200 mg as an initial IV bolus can be given, with 25-30 mg oral hydrocortisone for chronic treatment, divided into morning and evening doses. Adrenal Insufficiency Media explanations.

stem: A 29-year-old man who has Marfan syndrome presents to the Emergency Department with shortness of breath and sudden-onset left-sided pleuritic chest pain. His chest X-ray shows a left-sided pneumothorax. Which of the following is the simplest way to estimate the size of the pneumothorax?
options: Distance from the lung apex to the thoracic cupola
Distance from the chest wall to peripheral lung edge at the level of the hilum
Measurement of the A-a gradient on blood-gas sampling
Oxygen saturation below 93% measured on heart rate oximetry
explanation: Distance from the lung edge to the chest wall at the level of the hilum is the preferred measure for a chest X- ray to determine pneumothorax size according to the British Thoracic Society(BTS) guidelines. The cut off under BTS guidelines for determining a significant pneumothorax in this case is 2 cm and drives differences in management between air aspiration and insertion of a chest drain. A 2.5 cm rim of air corresponds to a pneumothorax of approximately 30%. External Links Management of spontaneous pneum.. bsuh.nhs.uk/library/wp-content/uploads.⋯.

stem: A 22-year-old woman presents to the Outpatient Department for review.She says that she is obsessed with her diet and has to exercise extreme self-control to manage her eating. On further questioning, she admits to eating more food in conjunction with emotional stressors. Thereis erosion of tooth enamel on examination of the mouth. Her body mass index(BMI) is 23 kg/m. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin(Hb) 107 g/L 115-155 g/L White cell count(WCC) 7.2×10/L 4-11×10/L Platelets(PLT) 203×10/L 150-400×10/L Sodium (Na+) 141 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/L Potassium (K+) 3.1 mmol/L 3.5-5.0 mmol/L Creatinine(Cr) 81μmol/L 50-120 μmol/L Which of the following is the most likely underlying diagnosis?
explanation: Clues leading to bulimia nervosa include the commentary about finding it difficult for the patient to control their eating, the BMl above the range for anorexia nervosa, the loss of tooth enamel, potentially related to stomach acid from vomiting and the hypokalaemia which could be related to vomiting or use of laxatives. ALL patients with suspected bulimia should be referred to an age-appropriate eating disorders clinic for assessment and advice on further management. Bulimia Nervosa Media explanations.

stem: A 74-year-old man is admitted to the Emergency Department following a syncopal episode. He reports that he has been passing dark motions over the past few days.His blood pressure is 90/60 mmHg and his heart rate is 100 bpm and regular. Which of the following is the most useful pointer towards upper gastrointestinal(GI) bleeding in this case?
explanation: Urea is the most specific biochemical marker for distinguishing upper from lower gastrointestinal (GI) haemorrhage; it has a specificity of 93% for differentiating between the two. This is because the blood meal, absorption of blood from the upper Gl tract, drives a marked increase in urea levels. Bleeding lower down the GI tract does not lead to the same urea elevation. Difficuty:Average.

stem: A 45-year-old woman presents to her General Practitioner (GP) with a urinary tract infection(UTI). She is currently being treated with trimethoprim. She feels much better and now has no symptoms, although the GP checked her bloods three days into treatment and noted a rise in creatinine from 85μmol/l to 119μmol/L. Which of the following is the likely cause of the rise in creatinine seen here?
options: Inhibition of tubular secretion of creatinine
explanation: The effect of trimethoprim in causing reversible inhibition of tubular secretion of creatinine is well described. Given the patient is well, it fits with the modest increase in serum creatinine seen here. In the event the GP measures it off therapy,it is likely to have returned to normal. When glomerular filtration rate(GFR) is measured rather than estimated using an inulin-based method, no reduction in GFR is seen. Difficuty:Average.

stem: A75-year-old woman is admitted to the Neurology Ward with a rapid cognitive decline over four weeks. She is now bedbound and mumbling incomprehensibly. She has dystonic movements and obvious myoclonus. Her electroencephalogram reveals periodic triphasic sharp waves on the background of generalised delta slowing. Which of the following is the most useful next investigation?
explanation: This patient's rapid mental deterioration with loss of walking, dystonic movements and myoclonus is typical of sporadic Creutzfeldt Jacob disease(CJD). Sporadic CJD is associated with 14-3-3 protein in the CSF and this therefore is the most useful next diagnostic step. New-variant CJD is not associated with the 14-3-3 protein. The EEG appearance seen here, with periodic spikes and delta slowing is typical of the underlying diagnosis. There is no treatment for either sporadic or new-variant CJD. Dificulty:Average.

stem: A58-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department with an acute flare of gout affecting his left knee. He normally takes allopurinol 100 mg daily and has heart failure and peptic ulcer disease for which he takes omeprazole. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin (Hb) 147 g/l 135-175 g/l White cell count (WCC) 7.2×10/L 4-11×10/L Platelets(PLT) 192×10/ 150-400×10/L Sodium(Na+) 143 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/L Potassium(K+) 4.5 mmol/L 3.5-5.0 mmol/L Creatinine (Cr) 90 μmol/L 50-120 μmol/L C-reactive protein (CRP) 55 mg/L 10 mg/l Urate 0.64 mmol/L 0.24-0.51 mmol/L Which of the following is the most appropriate way to treat the patient's acute gout?
explanation: This patient has heart failure and peptic ulcer disease, which are relative contraindications both for naproxen and prednisolone. Topical ibuprofen is not effective in this situation and increased allopurinol does not affect acute gout significantly. This leaves colchicine as the intervention of choice. Colchicine disrupts tubulin formation and impacts particularly on white blood cell activity, downregulating inflammation in acute gout. The dose is adjusted to gain control of symptoms and is usually started at 0.5 mg 2-4 times/day. Gout Media explanations.
