stem: A 67-year-old woman presents to the Emergency Department following a collapse at the local supermarket. She has chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and has recently been treated with clarithromycin for an exacerbation. Her partner tells you she has had diarrhoea for a few days. Heart rate is 95 bpm and regular, blood pressure is 90/70mmHg. There is wheeze on auscultation of the chest, with crackles at both bases. On examination, she has a short run of polymorphic ventricular tachycardia (VT) on the monitor. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin(Hb) 122 g/l 115-155 g/l White cell count(WCC) 8.9×10/L 4-11×10/L Platelets (PLT) 301×10/L 150-400×10/L Sodium (Na+) 143 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/L Potassium (K+) 3.6 mmol/L 3.5-5.0 mmol/L Creatinine (Cr) 132μmol/L 50-120 μmol/l Electrocardiogram(ECG) QTc 540 ms 450 ms Which of the following is the most appropriate intervention for this patient's arrhythmia?
explanation: This patient has Torsade de pointes VT, most likely as a result of diarrhoea, leading to a reduction in magnesium, combined with prescription of clarithromycin, which is known to prolong the QT interval. Similar to treatment of acute asthma, a dose of 2 g of magnesium sulphate is usually given over 20 minutes. It can be repeated as short as 10-15 minutes later. The clarithromycin should be withdrawn. Ventricular Tachycardia-Polymorphic explanations.

stem: A 19-year-old woman is referred to the Gastroenterology Clinic with anaemia. She has a normal menstrual cycle and takes the progesterone-only pill. She suffers from intermittent diarrhoea and abdominal bloating but puts this down to her diet. Her body mass index is 23 kg/m. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin(Hb) 89 g/l 115-155 g/l White cell count(WCC) 5.9×10/L 4-11×10/L Platelets(PLT) 203×10/L 150-400×10/L Sodium(Na+) 142 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/L Potassium (K+) 4.5 mmol/L 3.5-5.0 mmol/L Creatinine (Cr) 92 μmol/L 50-120 μmol/L Ferritin 8 ng/ml 10-300 ng/ml Which of the following is the most appropriate next investigation?
options: Upper gastrointestinal (GI) endoscopy with small-bowel biopsy
explanation: This patient has unexplained iron-deficiency anaemia in the presence of episodic diarrhoea and a normal menstrual cycle. According to guidelines, coeliac disease should be excluded and measurement of anti-TTG antibodies is the first step. Anti-TTG antibodies have a sensitivity of over 90% in patients with untreated coeliac disease, but over 70% of patients with coeliac disease who avoid gluten become TTG negative. Endoscopy with small-bowel biopsy to confirm the diagnosis follows anti-TTG testing. Coeliac Disease Media explanations.

stem: A 69-year-old man presents to the Renal Clinic for his 3-month review and complains of bilateral pitting ankle oedema. He is otherwise well. He has a past medical history of angina and resistant hypertension. He takes a number of oral medications. Which of the following is the most likely cause of his ankle swelling?
explanation: Doxazosin is an alpha-blocker which leads to peripheral vasodilatation. Consequently,1-10% of patients taking the medication report pitting oedema of the lower limb. This is dose-dependent and is more likely to occur at higher doses. Alpha-blockers also increase the risk of cardiac failure and are not recommended for use in any patients with a reduced ejection fraction. There are usually considered a third- or fourth-line blood-pressure-lowering option because of their adverse-event profile. Difficulty.

stem: A 28-year-old motorcyclist presents to the Outpatient Department some three months after a road traffic collision. Examination of the right upper limb reveals winging of the scapula. Which nerve is most likely to have been injured?
explanation: The long-thoracic nerve arises from the anterior rami of the C5,C6 and C7 spinal nerves. It can be subject to injury, particularly when there are twisting and tearing forces such as those occurring in a motorcycle accident. The nerve innervates the serratus anterior muscle, paralysis of which results in winging of the scapula. Difficutty.

stem: The role of endothelin-1 and the endothelin-A and -B receptors in health and disease are being examined. Which of the following is most accurate with respect to endothelin and its receptors?
options: Antagonism of endothelin-A receptors causes vasoconstriction
Agonism of endothelin-B1 receptors leads to natriuresis
Agonism of endothelin-B1 receptors blocks release of nitric oxide
Endothelin-1 levels are reduced in portal hypertension patients
explanation: Agonism of the B1 receptor leads to natriuresis, diuresis and vasodilation, the vasodilation is driven by release of nitric oxide. These mechanisms together lead to a small reduction in systolic blood pressure and a greater reduction in blood pressure through the pulmonary vascular bed. The differential effects of A vs B1 receptor agonism has driven the development of selective A-receptor antagonists. Difficulty.

stem: A 34-year-old woman presents to the Renal Department after receiving a kidney transplant. She is cytomegalovirus(CMV) negative, whereas the donor kidney is from a CMV-positive donor. Which of the following is the most appropriate prophylactic regimen against CMV infection?
explanation: Valganciclovir is the prophylactic agent of choice for solid organ transplants which carry a high risk of cytomegalovirus (CMV) infection occurring in the recipient, usually when the donor is CMV positive and the recipient is CMV negative. A dose of 450 mg once a day is usually prescribed.

stem: A 20-year-old man is referred to the Renal Clinic after the sudden death of his father from a subarachnoid haemorrhage. The father was also diagnosed with multiple renal cysts, haematuria and progressive renal failure. Which of the following is the optimal initial screening investigation for the son?
explanation: Ultrasound is able to detect renal cysts which are larger than 1-1.5 cm in diameter. Sensitivity for polycystic kidney disease is said to be 100% over the age of 20. False negatives can occur below this age. Liver cysts may well also be identified on the ultrasound scan.

stem: A34-year-old woman who is known to have depression presents to the Outpatient Department complaining of weight gain, galactorrhoea and nausea over the past few weeks. She has not had a menstrual period for six months. Medication includes amitriptyline, olanzapine and as-required (PRN) diazepam. Her blood pressure is 122/72 mmHg and her heart rate is 63 bpm and regular. Visual field examination is normal. Her body mass index(BMI) is 32 kg/m. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin(Hb) 105 g/l 115-155 g/l White cell count (WCC) 6.9×10/L 4-11×10/L Platelets(PLT) 302×10/L 150-400×10/L Sodium (Na+) 142 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/L Potassium(K+) 4.0 mmol/L 3.5-5.0 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 90 μmol/L 50-120 μmol/L Thyroid-stimulating 3.5 U/L 0.5-4.5 U/L hormone(TSH) Follicle-stimulating 2 U/L 1.0-9.0 IU/L hormone (FSH) Prolactin 2750 IU 59-619 IU Glucose (fasting) 5.7 mmol/L 7.0 mmol/l Which of the following is the most likely cause of her elevated prolactin?
explanation: Hyperprolactinaemia and prolactinoma Media explanations The weight gain here, coupled with six months of absent menses raise the possibility of pregnancy. In pregnancy, prolactin can be elevated to up to seven times the upper limit of the normal range by week 38. Follicle-stimulating hormone is suppressed, which also fits with the diagnosis. She is also mildly anaemic. The absence of a visual field defect rules out a large(macro) prolactinoma. A pregnancy test is the logical next step; in the event it is negative then magnetic resonance imaging of the pituitary should be performed to look for a microprolactinoma.

stem: A 62-year-old woman who has diabetes presents to the Emergency Department with right-left disorientation, finger agnosia,agraphia and acalculia. She is thought to have suffered a parietal lobe stroke. Which artery supplies the parietal lobe?
explanation: The parietal lobe receives blood supply from the middle cerebral, anterior cerebral and posterior cerebral arteries. The latter two arteries supply the medial parietal lobe. To produce symptoms, the occlusion is usually after the anastomosis with the anterior communicating artery.

stem: A 74-year-old man who has deteriorated suddenly is reviewed on the Cardiology Ward. He is three days' post myocardial infarction for which he received two stents and had been recovering well. He is now very short of breath and has become hypotensive but denies chest pain. His heart rate is 98 bpm and regular and his blood pressure is 95/70 mmHg. There are crackles to the midzones bilaterally on auscultation of the chest and O saturation is 93% on 6 litres of O. He has a pansystolic murmur radiating to the axilla. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's symptoms?
explanation: This patient has acute mitral regurgitation, manifested by the pansystolic murmur radiating to the axilla and development of left-ventricular failure. Mitral regurgitation can occur as a result of myocardial infarction related to remodelling, or as a result of papillary muscle rupture and has been described as presenting 1-14 days after infarct. Echocardiogram with colour-flow doppler is the initial investigation of choice, with surgical valve replacement the most appropriate intervention. Mitral regurgitation post myocardial infarction is an independent predictor of severe heart failure and death.

stem: A72-year-old woman is admitted to Acute Medicine Ward with acute kidney injury. While she is waiting to be seen, her blood results are phoned through from the lab. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin(Hb) 109 g/L 115-155 g/l White cell count (WCC) 9.1×10/L 4-11×10/L Platelets(PLT) 191×10/L 150-400×10/L Sodium(Na+) 143 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/L Potassium (K+) 7.6 mmol/L 3.5-5.0 mmol/L Creatinine (Cr) 421μmol/L 50-120 μmol/L Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
explanation: This patient has renal failure with life-threatening hyperkalaemia.10 ml of 9.5% calcium gluconate intravenously significantly reduces the incidence of life-threatening arrhythmia while further measures can be taken to reduce potassium. The bolus of calcium gluconate can be repeated after 10-15 minutes. It should be given ahead of other therapies including insulin and dextrose. Calcium works by reinforcing the cell membrane against destabilisation.

stem: A 24-year-old woman presents to the Emergency Department with an asthma exacerbation and is started on prednisolone 40 mg daily. Which of the following modes of prednisolone will improve this patient's asthma symptoms?
options: Decreased transcription of acetylcholine receptor genes
Decreased transcription of beta-2 receptor genes
explanation: The primary function of the glucocorticoid receptor is to regulate expression of pro-inflammatory and anti- inflammatory genes. Once agonism of the receptor occurs by prednisolone, the activated glucocorticoid receptor complex up-regulates the expression of anti-inflammatory peptides in the nucleus and reduces the expression of pro-inflammatory proteins in the cytosol. It does this by preventing the translocation of other transcription factors from the cytosol into the nucleus.

stem: A 78-year-old woman presents to the Elderly Care Ward. She has symptoms of Clostridium difficile infection in the past two days. Sheis the third person to present with these symptoms while being on the ward. How should surfaces be cleaned in the ward to reduce the spread of C.difficile?
explanation: Dilute bleach solution, diluted to 1000 parts per million available chlorine is recommended by guidelines for cleaning of areas which may be contaminated by C. difficile. This is because chlorine-based bleaches are sporicidal.

stem: A 65-year-old man is referred to the Urgent Ophthalmology Clinic because of bilateral central scotomas noted at a routine optometry appointment. Intraocular pressure is raised at 23 mmHg and there is bilateral optic-disc cupping. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial intervention?
explanation: This patient has raised intraocular pressure with optic-disc cupping and a central scotoma. This is consistent with chronic open-angle glaucoma. Topical beta-blockers such as timolol are a first-line intervention for glaucoma, particularly when patients are unsuitable for treatment with a prostaglandin analogue; they reduce the production of aqueous by the ciliary body by inhibiting beta-receptors. Prostaglandin analogues are another initial option recommended by National Institute for Health and Care Excellence guidelines; they increase aqueous outflow via the uveoscleral route.

stem: A 29-year-old drug addict is admitted to the Emergency Department with tetanus thought to be related to injection technique. She has ankle clonus. Contraction of which muscle is the cause of ankle clonus?
explanation: The gastrocnemius muscle is responsible for plantar flexion of the foot.It is also the muscle which contracts when individuals suffer from ankle clonus. This is associated with increased tone and occurs due to an upper motor neurone lesion.

stem: A 23-year-old man with a strong family history of diabetes is reviewed in the Genetics Clinic. There is concern that the patient has an inherited syndrome associated with severe insulin resistance. In which part of the cell is the insulin receptor located?
explanation: The insulin receptor is a transmembrane receptor which is activated by insulin. Insulin-like growth factor 1 (IGF-1) and IGF-2.Insulin plays a key role in glucose homeostasis, regulating both carbohydrate and fat metabolism.It is a tyrosine kinase receptor, activation of which leads to the translocation of the glut-4 transporter to the plasma membrane which allows an influx of glucose. It also stimulates synthesis of glycogen and fatty acids.

stem: The results of a cardiovascular outcome study of a new agent for the treatment of type ll diabetes is being reviewed. It appears to show a reduction of 20% in major adverse cardiovascular events. Up to 15% of patients who take the drug discontinue therapy because of gastrointestinal adverse effects. Which of the following is the most appropriate analysis to establish the risk-benefit profile of the new drug?
explanation: The intention to treat (ITT) analysis includes all patients post randomisation. This provides a true estimate of the risk-benefit for a particular drug because patients who have dropped out due to a tolerability issue may have benefited or been harmed by their short period on therapy. The ITT analysis is traditionally used by regulatory agencies for licensing a medicine.

stem: A 64-year-old man who has hypertension presents to the Emergency Department with sudden-onset tearing central chest pain radiating to his back for the past hour. Apart from hypertension, he is usually well. His blood pressure is 165/90 mmHg in the right arm and 135/85 mmHg in the left arm. His heart rate is 92 bpm and regular. There are no signs of cardiac failure on auscultation of the chest. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin (Hb) 129 g/l 135-175 g/l White cell count (WCC) 6.1×10/L 4-11×10/L Platelets(PLT) 201×10/L 150-400×10/L Sodium(Na+) 138 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/L Potassium(K+) 4.5 mmol/L 3.5-5.0 mmol/L Creatinine (Cr) 123 μmol/L 50-120 μmol/L Computed tomography (CT) Type B aortic dissection aortogram Which of the following is the most appropriate way to control this patient's blood pressure?
explanation: bnf.nice.org.uk/drug/labetalol-hydrochlo..

stem: A 35-year-old woman presents to the General Practitioner with lethargy,thirst and bony pains over the past few months. She has also gained weight recently which she puts down to eating more to relieve indigestion. Her blood pressure is 142/88mmHg and her heart rate is 80 bpm and regular. Her body mass index is 29 kg/m. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin (Hb) 122 g/l 115-155 g/l White cell count (WCC) 6.1×10/L 4-11×10/L Platelets (PLT) 172×10/L 150-400×10/L Sodium(Na+) 142 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/L Potassium (K+) 3.7 mmol/l 3.5-5.0 mmol/L Creatinine (Cr) 90 μmol/L 50-120 μmol/L Calcium(Ca+) 2.95 mmol/l 2.1-2.65 mmol/L Phosphate (PO-) 0.7 mmol/L 0.8-1.5 mmol/l Parathyroid hormone(PTH) 8.2 pmol/L 1.6-6.9 pmol/L Multiple endocrine neoplasia type 1 (MEN1) is suspected. Which of the following features is expected to be present?
explanation: Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia Media explanations Multiple endocrine neoplasia type 1(MEN1) is characterised by 4-gland parathyroid hyperplasia and in 70% of patients, pancreatic endocrine tumours are also seen. Over 60% of tumours are gastrinomas which can lead to the development of multiple peptic ulcers. Insulinomas are much rarer, seen in around 30% of patients with MEN1. Patients also present with multiple cutaneous lesions including angiofibromas, collagenomas and lipomas. Carcinoid tumours are found in around 10% of MEN1 patients but are rarely symptomatic.

stem: An 18-year-old man is referred to the Haematology Clinic. He has longstanding haemolytic anaemia and symptomatic splenomegaly. His father and brother suffer from the same condition. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin(Hb) 110 g/L(spherocytes seen on blood film) 135-175 g/L Mean cell volume(MCV) 102 fl 80-100 fl White cell count (WCC) 7.2×10/L 4-11×10/L Platelets(PLT) 302×10/L 150-400×10/L Sodium(Na+) 141 mmol/l 135-145 mmol/L Potassium(K+) 4.5 mmol/L 3.5-5.0 mmol/L Creatinine (Cr) 90 μmol/L 50-120 μmol/L Which of the following is the gold-standard investigation to confirm the cause of this patient's haemolytic anaemia?
explanation: This patient has hereditary spherocytosis, caused by a red-cell-membrane defect. The most common defect in Europeans is a combined spectrin and ankyrin deficiency;this is present in 40-65% of patients. The optimal test to confirm hereditary spherocytosis is cryohaemolysis and eosin 5-maleimide (EMA) binding (EMA binding is a flow cytometry test seen as the gold standard for diagnosing the disease). Hereditary Spherocytosis Media explanations The defective red cells are preferentially sequestered and destroyed in the spleen, which leads to chronic haemolytic anaemia. Eventually, this leads to symptomatic splenomegaly and the haemolytic process over time results in an increased risk of gallstones. A planned splenectomy is, therefore,typical in the late teenage years, after which patients require antibiotic prophylaxis.

stem: An audit has been carried out about the use of dialysis in patients with overdose in the hospital. What pharmacokinetic property is associated with the highest level of clearance by dialysis?
explanation: Water solubility is a key to high levels of drug clearance via haemodialysis. Drugs are then removed via counter-current flow across a semi-permeable membrane. In addition to high water solubility, compounds need to be maintained in the plasma at a high enough concentration to establish a gradient across the dialysis membrane. This means that some compounds such as digoxin which have high levels of water solubility but also a large volume of distribution are actually quite poorly cleared by dialysis.

stem: A 74-year-old man who has type ll diabetes and hypertension presents to the Emergency Department with sudden-onset severe nausea, vomiting and vertigo. He has ataxia, nystagmus, dysarthria and dysphagia. There is left-sided Horner syndrome and right-sided loss of pain and temperature sensation over the trunk and limbs. Where is the arterial occlusion most likely to be that has caused this patient's symptoms?
explanation: This patient has features of lateral medullary syndrome, which most commonly occurs due to occlusion of the vertebral artery. Symptoms can include: Difficulty: Difficult · vertigo, falling to the side of the lesion, diplopia and nystagmus in all directions · autonomic dysfunction including ipsilateral Horner syndrome and hiccoughs · loss of pain and temperature sensation over the contralateral side of the body · ipsilateral bulbar muscle weakness which leads to hoarseness, dysphonia, dysphagia and dysarthria and decreased gag reflex. Magnetic resonance imaging with diffusion-weighted imaging is the best way to identify the area of infarction within the lateral medulla.

stem: A 23-year-old man who is diagnosed with type I diabetes presents to the Outpatient Department feeling unwell. He is sweating profusely and slurring his speech. A finger prick glucose test returns a glucose level of 2.8 mmol/L. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
explanation: This patient is still conscious, meaning that oral therapy with dextrose gel is the most appropriate next intervention. In the event it is ineffective in relieving symptoms,1mg of IM glucagon is the most appropriate step. If recovery of symptoms occurs, then glucose should be checked after 15minutes.In the event that it is still below 4.0 mmol/L, the oral dextrose treatment should be repeated.

stem: A71-year-old woman presents to the Outpatient Department with lethargy, shortness of breath, pins and needles in her hands and feet and mild peripheral limb weakness. She does not take any medication apart from amlodipine for hypertension and a salbutamol inhaler. Her blood pressure is 118/82 mmHg and heart rate is 85 bpm and regular. She has absent ankle and knee jerks and 4/5 power weakness affecting both ankles and loss of vibration and joint position sense affecting her hands and feet. Her body mass index is 24 kg/m. nvestigations: Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin (Hb) 99 g/l 115-155 g/l Mean corpuscular volume(MCV) 103 fl 80-100 fl White cell count (WCC) 6.1×10/L 4-11×10/L Platelets(PLT) 293×10/L 150-400×10/L Sodium(Na+) 142 mmol/l 135-145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 3.7 mmol/L 3.5-5.0 mmol/L Creatinine (Cr) 90 μmol/L 50-120 μmol/l Which of the following is the most useful next investigation?
explanation: Peripheral motor and sensory polyneuropathy in a patient with anaemia and raised mean corpuscular volume suggests possible vitamin B2 deficiency. A serum cobalamin of less than 148 pmol/L is considered the cut-off point to diagnose 97% of patients with vitamin B2 deficiency. An autoantibody screen to rule out pernicious anaemia is the next step after confirming vitamin B12 levels are low, looking for intrinsic-factor antibodies. Intramuscular vitamin B12 injections are the treatment of choice, given three times a week for the first two weeks and then 1 mg every three months.

stem: A 56-year-old man who is thought to have diabetic nephropathy presents to the Outpatient Department to discuss the results of a renal biopsy. Which of the following would be an expected finding?
explanation: Three key findings are present on kidney biopsy in diabetic nephropathy. These include: · glomerular basement membrane thickening · mesangial expansion · arteriolar hyalinosis. Diabetic nephropathy is usually diagnosed based on clinical features. Patients do not normally receive a renal biopsy unless other diagnoses are considered.

stem: A54-year-old man is admitted to the hospital with anti-glomerular basement membrane disease and has haemoptysis with acute renal failure. He is commenced on high-dose corticosteroids and cyclophosphamide. Which of the following best describes a primary mode of action of cyclophosphamide?
explanation: Cyclophosphamide is thought to have an inhibitory effect on B cells, CD4+T cells and to a lesser extent on CD8+ T cells. It is not clear whether the cytostatic action of cyclophosphamide is entirely dependent on the alkylation of deoxyribonucleic acid(DNA) or if other mechanisms play a role, such as inhibition of chromatin transformation or inhibition of DNA polymerases.In animal studies, B cells were reduced by up to 75% by day seven following a single dose of the agent.

stem: A 57-year-old man is diagnosed with essential hypertension and started on amlodipine 5mg to be taken once daily. He is concerned about possible adverse effects of his medication. Which of the following is the patient most likely to suffer from?
explanation: Headaches are commonly seen in patients who are prescribed amlodipine and other dihydropyridine calcium antagonists. This is likely as a result of vasodilatation. Other effects commonly seen include oedema and palpitations. Many patients report facial flushing as a result of amlodipine. The lower dose of amlodipine,(5 mg) has similar efficacy to 10 mg, but with a more favourable adverse-effect profile. This prompts the addition of a different class of antihypertensive in the event 5mg does not control blood pressure, rather than increasing the dose.

stem: A 27-year-old man is brought to the Emergency Department by his partner.He has recently returned from Thailand where he was working at a dog sanctuary. He has a severe sore throat, has difficulty swallowing and is unable to walk due to lower limb weakness. His temperature is 38.2℃, blood pressure is 110/80 mmHg and his heart rate is 80 bpm and regular.He has pharyngitis with a pseudomembrane, neck oedema and cervical lymphadenopathy. He has obvious 3/5 power weakness affecting both lower limbs, with diminished reflexes. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Q. Answered Flagged Diphtheria is very rarely seen but should always be consideredin patients who present with pharyngitis,a pseudomembrane and flaccid paralysis. The clue here is the visit to the Far East, where more cases of diphtheria are seen and working with dogs, which may carry the diphtheria bacterium and could pass to humans. Macrolide antibiotics are the intervention of choice and diphtheria vaccination should be given during the convalescent period to ensure there is a strong antitoxin antibody response. Ventilatory support may be required and myocarditis is associated with prolonged morbidity in patients with diphtheria. Mortality approaches 5-10% overall.

stem: A 62-year-old man with end-stage pancreatic cancer presents to the Palliative Care Clinic requesting buprenorphine to be started in addition to his morphine modified-release tablets, as a feels these are not controlling his pain. Which of the following is most likely to happen when they are used in combination?
options: No effect on top of his morphine
explanation: Buprenorphine is a partial agonist opioid agent, acting at the mu-opioid receptor. It also has antagonistic activity at the kappa-opioid receptor. It should be used cautiously with other opioids including morphine and in combination with sedative antihistamines and anxiolytics. This is because the combination can result in significant CNS depression. If the patient wishes to switch, or it is deemed clinically appropriate, the buprenorphine should be started at the lowest patch dose available and supplemented with short-acting morphine as required.

stem: A71-year-old retired General Practitioner is referred to the Outpatient Department for management of hypertension. He asks about the effects of ageing on the cardiovascular system. Which of the following statements most accurately describes the relationship between cardiovascular physiology and ageing?
options: Diastolic blood pressure (BP) increases more than systolic BP
explanation: Pulse pressure widens with increasing age because systolic blood pressure increases, whereas diastolic blood pressure stays the same or gradually falls. This is related to arterial stiffness which increases over time. Increased arterial stiffness causes a rise in heart rate wave velocity, which causes the reflected wave from one heartbeat to add to the forward wave of blood from the subsequent beat, augmenting systolic output.

stem: A 24-year-old woman who has had type I diabetes for the past 19 years presents to the Outpatient Department for her routine follow up. She uses an insulin pump to control her blood sugar but takes no other medication. Her blood pressure is 110/70 mmHg. She has loss of fine-touch sensation in both feet. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin(Hb) 132 g/l 115-155 g/L White cell count (WCC) 7.1×10/L 4-11×10/L Platelets(PLT) 301×10/L 150-400×10/L Sodium(Na+) 142 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/L Potassium (K+) 4.5 mmol/L 3.5-5.0 mmol/L Creatinine (Cr) 80 μmol/L 50-120 μmol/L Glycosylated haemoglobin 48 mmol/mol 48 mmol/mol (HbA1c) Urinary albumin-creatinine ratio 10 mg/mmol, (repeated twice) 3 mg/mmol Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
explanation: Both angiotensin-converting enzyme(ACE) inhibitors and angiotensin receptor blockers are proven to reduce the progression of diabetic nephropathy, the likely cause of this patient's albuminuria. ALthough the blood pressure is normal, ACE inhibitors have still been shown to reduce deterioration in the glomerular filtration rate over time. Guidelines recommend starting an agent such as ramipril and uptitrating as high as is tolerated. If this patient wishes to try for a child, the ramipril should be discontinued,as it is teratogenic.

stem: A72-year-old woman presents to the Emergency Department complaining of bilateral shoulder pain and stiffness which has steadily worsened over the past three weeks. She also has pain in her hips. The pain lasts for more than 45minutes each morning and is not really relieved by paracetamol. She has hypertension for which she takes ramipril 5mg daily. Examination confirms bilateral upper arm tenderness and that her shoulder movement is severely limited by the pain. nvestigations: Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin (Hb) 120 g/l 115-155 g/l White cell count (WCC) 7.1×10/L 4-11×10/L Platelets(PLT) 291×10/L 150-400×10/L Sodium(Na+) 142 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/L Potassium (K+) 4.3 mmol/L 3.5-5.0 mmol/L Creatinine (Cr) 99 μmol/L 50-120 μmol/l Erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) 89 mm/h 10 mm/h C-reactive protein (CRP) 102 mg/l 10 mg/l Which of the following is the most appropriate intervention?
explanation: This patient has shoulder and hip-girdle pain and stiffness which is severe and lasts for more than 45 minutes per day. Given her age and the marked elevation in ESR, this is consistent with a diagnosis of polymyalgia rheumatica(PMR). In this situation a prednisolone dose of 15 mg per day is recommended for the first three weeks of treatment followed by gradual tapering. Any symptoms of temporal headache should prompt use of a higher prednisolone dose. A rapid improvement in symptoms of PMR is expected within 48 hours of starting corticosteroid therapy.

stem: A72-year-old man is found unconscious while on the Respiratory Ward recovering from right lower-lobe pneumonia. He has suffered a cardiac arrest. The ward defibrillator shows ventricular fibrillation and one direct current shock is delivered but does not restore sinus rhythm. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
options: Give two further direct current shocks
Immediately resume cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) for two minutes
explanation: This patient has been found in cardiac arrest and there is no indication how long he has arrested for. In this case, guidelines recommend only a single shock(as had been given),followed by a return to a further two minutes of cardiopulmonary resuscitation. Cardiopulmonary resuscitation is given with a ratio of 30 chest compressions:2 breaths. While cardiopulmonary resuscitation is taking place, other members of the team should assess for reversible causes of cardiac arrest,including measurement of arterial blood gases,ruling out causes of hypovolaemia and assessing for possible pneumothorax.

stem: A 29-year-old woman who takes sildenafil for primary pulmonary hypertension presents to the Outpatient Department with a positive pregnancy test. Her last investigations suggested that her pulmonary artery pressure was well controlled. She believes that she is around eight weeks'pregnant and wants to continue the pregnancy. Which of the following is the most suitable management for this patient?
explanation: Adding low molecular weight heparin is essential in patients with primary pulmonary hypertension who get pregnant. This is to reduce the risk of pulmonary embolism(PE), given that this is a major cause of death in this situation. Her pulmonary hypertension is well controlled at present, so there is no need to add other therapies to control pulmonary artery pressure. Antiplatelet therapies are ineffective in reducing the risk of PE. Warfarin is not recommended for anticoagulation in pregnancy according to the Royal College of Obstetrics and Gynaecology green guide.

stem: A 29-year-old man presents to the Oncology Clinic following left orchidectomy for a testicular seminoma. Unfortunately, his chest X-ray has shown evidence of metastases. Which tumour marker is most likely to be elevated?
explanation: Lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) is less specific for testicular carcinoma versus HCG and AFP but AFP is never raised in seminomas and HCG is only raised 15% of the time in seminomas.LDH is correlated with high tumour burden in seminoma and given this patient has lung metastases it is the correct answer here.

stem: A 64-year-old man presents to the Outpatient Department with angina. Current medication includes bisoprolol and aspirin. He gets pain 3-4 times per week while going for a walk with his dog. He smokes 15 cigarettes per day. His blood pressure is 143/80 mmHg, heart rate is 65 bpm and regular. There are no murmurs and he has a coarse wheeze on auscultation of the chest consistent with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin(Hb) 141 g/l 135-175 g/l White cell count(WCC) 6.2×109/L 4-11×10/L Platelets (PLT) 301×10/L 150-400×10/L Sodium(Na+) 142 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/L Potassium (K+) 4.4 mmol/L 3.5-5.0 mmol/L Creatinine (Cr) 92 μmol/L 50-120 μmol/L Low-density lipoprotein (LDL) cholesterol 2.7 mmol/L 1.8 mmol/L Cardiac computed tomography (CT) calcium 410 angstroms 100 angstroms scoring Which of the following is the most appropriate next intervention to improve his long-term oucomes?
explanation: This patient's calcium score is significantly elevated. The level 400 is the cut off for severe risk. Mild-to- normal calcium burden within the coronary arteries is signified by an angstrom score of less than 100. Low- density lipoprotein (LDL) cholesterol is also significantly above target at 2.7 mmol/l versus a threshold of 1.8 mmol/L. Atorvastatin should be introduced and titrated to a high dose, if possible, to ensure that LDL cholesterol is within the high-risk threshold of 1.8 mmol/L.

stem: You are asked to review a 48-year-old man who has been admitted to the Surgical Ward with acute pancreatitis. He has deteriorated over the past three hours with worsening shortness of breath. His blood pressure is 122/82 mmHg, heart rate is 88 bpm and regular. He has bilateral inspiratory crackles on auscultation of the chest. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin(Hb) 111 g/l 135-175 g/l White cell count (WCC) 12.9×10/L 4-11×109/L Platelets(PLT) 129×10/ 150-400×10/L Sodium(Na+) 136 mmol/l 135-145 mmol/L Potassium(K+) 3.6 mmol/L 3.5-5.0 mmol/L Creatinine (Cr) 132μmol/l 50-120μmol/L Partial pressure of oxygen(PaO) 8.1 kPa (on 60% O) 10.6 kPa (air) Partial pressure of carbon dioxide 5.5 kPa 4.6-6.0 kPa (PaCO) Chest X-ray (CXR) Dense, patchy shadowing across both lung fields Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
explanation: Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome explanations This patient has non-cardiogenic pulmonary oedema following acute pancreatitis, consistent with acute respiratory distress syndrome(ARDS). The maintained blood pressure, crackles on auscultation of the chest and patchy shadowing in the presence of patchy opacification on the chest X-ray in the presence of marked hypoxia is consistent with the diagnosis. Continuous positive airway pressure therapy is the initial intervention of choice, with progression to ventilation indicated when PaO is below 8.3 kPa despite 60% O and PaCO rises above 6 kPa. Patients should be escalated to critical care to receive this treatment.

stem: A 20-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department with a rash for the past three days, a fever and symptoms of a cold. He reveals that he refuses vaccinations because he does not believe in them.On examination, he has a generalised morbiliform rash and small red spots opposite the second molar teeth on examination of the buccal mucosa. His temperature is 38.2℃, heart rate is 92 bpm and regular and blood pressure is 105/82 mmHg. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Q. Answered Flagged This patient's coryzal symptoms coupled with a measles-type rash for three days or more and Koplik's spots on examination of the buccal mucosa, fits with a diagnosis of measles. Unfortunately, his lack of belief in vaccination raises the possibility that his childhood vaccinations, including measles-mumps-rubella(MMR) may have been omitted by his parents. The rash begins to fade after 3-4 days in the order of where it first appeared, often leaving behind brown skin discolouration. Management is supportive, complications can include otitis media and secondary bacterial pneumonia.

stem: A32-year-old woman is referred to the Rheumatology Clinic with multiple joint pains affecting her hands, feet, wrists, ankles, elbows and knees over the past ten weeks. Despite her General Practitioner prescribing naproxen, her pains have not improved. She has no skin rashes and has suffered from intermittent pleuritic chest pains and fevers over the past few months. Which of the following would be expected on examination of the patient's hands?
explanation: Early rheumatoid arthritis is associated with active synovitis affecting the proximal interphalangeal joints and the metacarpophalangeal joints. More established rheumatoid arthritis is associated with tendon changes which result in swan-necking and boutonniere's deformity. Given this patient has very early disease, only swelling and stiffness is likely to be found. Her symptoms merit a short course of prednisolone to control them and over the long-term, she should be established on methotrexate.

stem: A72-year-old man presents to the Outpatient Department with his wife. He has worsening short-term memory, is no longer able to do the crossword and is bumping into things. According to his wife, he occasionally gets up at 03:00 am and has been seeing people in the kitchen who are not there. His General Practitioner had trialled risperidone to help his behaviour at night, but this affected his ability to walk. The patient has a slight tremor, more marked on the right-hand side than the left of the upper and lower limb and muscular rigidity. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Lewy body dementia presents with memory loss, progressive loss of spatial awareness and visual hallucinations. Symptoms may fluctuate on a day-to-day basis and there are features of mild Parkinson's disease on neurological examination. Patients respond very badly to antipsychotics with respect to a worsening of any underlying movement disorder, as has been seen here. Typical agents used for Parkinson's such as L-dopa may have limited impact on improving mobility, while worsening visual hallucinations.

stem: A 20-year-old woman presents to the Emergency Department complaining of headaches and a mild fever. She also has swollen lymph nodes in her left axilla. She has crusted erythematous lesions on the back of her left hand which have been caused by scratches from a neighbour's cat. Which of the following is the most likely cause for the patient's symptoms?
explanation: This patient has symptoms of cat-scratch fever, which is caused by B.henselae. The headaches, fever, regional lymphadenopathy and crusted lesions on the hand support the diagnosis. In patients without immunocompromise the condition is usually self-Limiting and resolves after a few days.Where symptoms are severe or if the patient is immunocompromised, azithromycin, ciprofloxacin and trimethoprim sulfamethoxazole are potential interventions. Patients should follow up with their primary care doctor after 2-6 months to confirm that their symptoms have resolved.

stem: A37-year-old woman presents to the Outpatient Department following a cervical biopsy for postcoital and intermenstrual bleeding. She is diagnosed with a squamous-cell cervical carcinoma. Which of the following viruses is most associated with the development of cervical carcinoma?
explanation: Human papillomavirus(HPV)-16 and HPV-18 are thought to play a role in the aetiology of 70% of cervical cancers, the majority of which are squamous-cell cancers. Two vaccines exist against these human papillomavirus subtypes. One of the vaccines also covers HPV-6 and HPV-11, meaning that it also reduces the incidence of genital warts. Both vaccines are more than 99% effective at preventing precancerous cervical lesions.

stem: The effects of a new dietary supplement on transit time in patients with irritable bowel syndrome are being reviewed. One group has been given the new supplement. The other group is taking a standard diet. Which of the following statistical tests is the most appropriate choice?
explanation: The input variable in this scenario is presence or absence of the new dietary supplement. The output variable, transit time, is quantitative and normally distributed. This makes t-testing the most appropriate statistical investigation. It is used to measure whether there is a difference between the means of the two populations (treated with the new agent or managed with standard of care).

stem: A 28-year-old man who has had several male sexual partners presents to the Dermatology Clinic with an erythematous greasy rash affecting the nasolabial folds in particular.There is some fine skin scaling, which is worse over the scalp and looks like dandruff and over his eyebrows. Examination reveals further erythematous patches over the sternum and flexural surfaces. Which of the following is the most useful next investigation?
explanation: This patient has seborrhoeic dermatitis, which explains the rash affecting his nose, eyebrows and scalp and the patches over the sternum and flexural areas. The disease is strongly associated with HIV infection and given that he is in a risk group for HIV,HIV testing is essential. It appears that the rash is worse with greater degrees of immunocompromise and it may well improve once antiretroviral therapy is instigated.

stem: A53-year-old pub owner presents to the General Practitioner complaining of chronic pain and stiffness affecting his right knee which has got much worse over the past few days. He has tried taking non-steroidal anti-inflammatory agents(NSAIDs) without much improvement. Examination reveals slight swelling of the right knee and pain on movement, with flexion limited to 60 degrees. Investigations: Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's knee pain? Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin(Hb) 143 g/L 135-175 g/l White cell count (WCC) 7.1×10/L 4-11×10/L Platelets(PLT) 189×109/L 150-400×10/L Sodium(Na+) 142 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 4.5 mmol/L 3.5-5.0 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 89 μmol/L 50-120 μmol/L C-reactive protein(CRP) 22 mg/L 10 mg/l Urate 0.49 mmol/L 0.24-0.51 mmol/L Right-knee X-ray Linear opacification of the articular cartilage
explanation: Pseudogout Media explanations The linear cartilage calcification is suggestive of chondrocalcinosis as a result of pyrophosphate crystal deposition, which has led to presentation with pseudogout. The urate being in the normal range and the more chronic nature of the patient's symptoms count against gout as an alternative diagnosis. The C-reactive protein is also only mildly elevated. Non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) are the mainstay of therapy for pseudogout and like gout, colchicine can be used where there are tolerability issues or thereis a contraindication to NSAIDs.

stem: A76-year-old woman presents to the Emergency Department after being found on the floor by her home help after 48 hours of diarrhoea and vomiting. She is drowsy and confused. Her blood pressure is 95/70 mmHg, heart rate is 95 bpm and regular. She has dry mucus membranes with increased skin turgor. Her abdomen is soft with active bowel sounds. She appears to be not moving her left-hand side. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin(Hb) 159 g/L 115-155 g/L White cell count(WCC) 12.9×10/L 4-11×10/L Platelets(PLT) 381×10/L 150-400×10/L Sodium (Na+) 156 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/L Potassium (K+) 5.8 mmol/L 3.5-5.0 mmol/L Creatinine(Cr) 291μmol/L 50-120 μmol/L Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's hypernatraemia?
explanation: This patient has elevated haemoglobin, elevated white blood cell count, a marked elevation in serum sodium and acute kidney injury. Given the nausea and vomiting, the most likely cause of her hypernatraemia is dehydration which may have been exacerbated by diuretic use.

stem: A49-year-old woman presents to the Emergency Department with abdominal pain, fever and rigours. She has been diagnosed with obesity and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), for which she receives oxygen. She has been unwell for the past 48 hours. Her blood pressure is 90/60 mmHg, her heart rate is 95 bpm and regular and her temperature is 38.2℃. She is very tender in the right upper quadrant. She is commenced on broad-spectrum antibiotics. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin (Hb) 109 g/l 115-155 g/l White cell count (WCC) 17.9×10/L 4-11×10/L Platelets(PLT) 172×10/L 150-400×10/L Sodium(Na+) 142 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/L Potassium (K+) 5.2 mmol/l 3.5-5.0 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 171 μmol/L 50-120 μmol/l Urgent ultrasound on Gallstone within the bile duct admission measured at 13 mm diameter, proximal duct dilatation Alanine transaminase (ALT) 131 U/L 1-40 U/L Alkaline phosphatase 341 U/L 30-130 U/L Bilirubin 41μmol/L 1-17 μmol/L Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
options: Endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography, sphincterotomy and stone removal
explanation: Gallstones and Gallbladder Disease explanations This patient has cholecystitis with a large gallstone obstructing the bile duct. As well as antibiotics, she requires an intervention to relieve the obstruction. Given the presence of Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease(COPD) severe enough to require home oxygen, she is unlikely to tolerate surgical intervention. This leaves endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography, with the potential for sphincterotomy and stone removal, the most appropriate next step. She has significant sepsis with renal impairment and antibiotics alone will not resolve her symptoms.

stem: A 29-year-old woman presents to her General Practitioner complaining of sudden shock-like pain and tingling over her left cheek that she says began six months earlier after a dental extraction on the left-hand side. She says the pain can last from seconds to minutes and often occurs multiple times a day, followed by long periods when she is pain free. Touching her face, cleaning her teeth and a cold wind are all potential triggers. Neurological examination is normal. Which of the following is the most likely cause of the patient's pain?
explanation: The paroxysms of shooting pain affecting the left cheek, triggered by touch or by cold are consistent with trigeminal neuralgia. Neurological examination is normal. Magnetic resonance imaging is required as part of the workup to rule out an anatomical cause for the pain such as an extracranial tumour, cerebellopontine- angle lesion or cavernous sinus mass. Carbamazepine is the initial intervention of choice for trigeminal neuralgia, with gabapentin and botulinum toxin other potential options.

stem: A 25-year-old man presents to the Outpatient Department for review. He has bilateral reduced acuity (particularly for near vision) over the past few months, loss of contrast sensitivity and abnormal dark adaptation. He has given up driving at night because of light glare. Fundoscopy reveals multiple discrete round,yellow deposits over the macular area. Which of the following is the most likely cause of the patient's deteriorating vision?
explanation: The clinical picture here with impaired near vision, impaired dark adaptation and optic-nerve drusen fits with macular degeneration. Although the patient is very young to develop macular degeneration, a number of gene mutations can lead to disease at an early age. These commonly involve the ABCA4 and ELOVL4 genes which code for light-sensing proteins within the retina. The mutations lead to a decreased ability to remove toxic metabolites from photoreceptor cells and a build-up of lipofuscin, with subsequent cell death.

stem: A51-year-old taxi driver presents to the Outpatient Department for review. He has decreased exercise tolerance, morning headaches and daytime sleepiness which has worsened over the last six months. He has hypertension for which he takes ramipril 10 mg and he smokes five cigarettes per day. He has had pneumonia twice over the past year. According to his wife, he snores heavily and gets up to pass urine three times per night. His blood pressure is 155/95 mmHg, heart rate is 75 bpm and regular. Auscultation of the chest reveals quiet breath sounds. His body mass index is 36 kg/m.His waist size is 116 cm. nvestigations: Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin(Hb) 161 g/l 135-175 g/L White cell count (WCC) 7.2×10/L 4-11×10/L Platelets(PLT) 281×10/L 150-400×10/L Sodium(Na+) 142 mmol/l 135-145 mmol/L Potassium (K+) 3.9 mmol/L 3.5-5.0 mmol/L Creatinine (Cr) 123 μmol/L 50-120 μmol/L Forced vital capacity(FVC) 2.8 litres 3.55 litres Which of the following is the most likely cause of the patient's symptoms?
explanation: The symptoms described here including snoring, enuresis, morning headaches and decreased exercise tolerance against a background of marked obesity, fit with a diagnosis of obesity hypoventilation syndrome.

stem: A 47-year-old man who has been diagnosed with bronchiectasis presents to the Acute Medical Ward with an exacerbation. He has a chronic cough and shortness of breath and he takes amlodipine for control of hypertension. His blood pressure is 132/82 mmHg, heart rate is 87 bpm and regular. He has coarse crackles at the right base on auscultation.Oxygen saturation is 93% measured on heart rate oximeter. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin(Hb) 151 g/l 135-175 g/l White cell count (WCC) 13.1×10/L 4-11×10/L Platelets(PLT) 203×10/L 150-400×10/L Sodium(Na+) 143 mmol/l 135-145 mmol/L Potassium(K+) 4.7 mmol/L 3.5-5.0 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 94μmol/L 50-120 μmol/L C-reactive protein (CRP) 231 mg/l 10 mg/l Sputum culture Pseudomonas aeruginosa Which of the following is most likely to reduce his risk of future exacerbations?
options: Inhaled long-acting beta-agonist and high-dose corticosteroid
explanation: Pseudomonas colonisation in bronchiectasis is associated with significantly worse short-term outcomes (exacerbations and days in hospital) and deteriorating lung function over a longer period. For this reason, attempted eradication of pseudomonas colonisation is the preferred intervention here, usually achieved with nebulised tobramycin±short-term intravenous antibiotics.

stem: A73-year-old man who takes inhaled triple therapy for coronary obstructive pulmonary disease(COPD) presents to the General Practitioner for review. He complains of shortness of breath despite being adherent to therapy. His blood pressure is 129/82 mmHg, heart rate is 78 bpm (atrial fibrillation). He has a hyperexpanded chest with quiet breath sounds. His body mass index is 23 kg/m.There is mild ankle swelling. Investigations: Which of the following is the strongest indication for long-term oxygen therapy (LTOT) in this patient? The wording of the indication for oxygen is reproduced below: Consider LTOT for people with COPD who do not smoke and who: · have a PaO below 7.3 kPa when stable or · have a PaO above 7.3 and below 8 kPa when stable, if they also have one or more of the following: Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease Media explanations o secondary polycythaemia o peripheral oedema o pulmonary hypertension.

stem: A 24-year-old woman presents to the Emergency Department with right iliac fossa pain, fever and joint pain over the last ten days. She has also suffered mild diarrhoea. She returned from a holiday in Thailand shortly before her symptoms began. She is usually well and takes no regular medication. Her temperature is 38.2℃ blood pressure is 105/72 mmHg, heart rate is 95 bpm and regular. She is very tender in the right iliac fossa and bowel sounds are normal. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin (Hb) 131 g/l 115-155 g/l White cell count(WCC) 13.3×10/L 4-11×10/L Platelets(PLT) 209×10/L 150-400×10/L Sodium(Na+) 142 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/L Potassium(K+) 4.5 mmol/L 3.5-5.0 mmol/L Creatinine (Cr) 82 μmol/L 50-120 μmol/L CRP 175 mg/l 10 mg/l Stool culture Gram-negative rod Which of the following is the most likely cause for this patient's abdominal pain?
explanation: Yersinia infection is often transmitted by eating undercooked pork,to which this patient may have been exposed on their trip to Thailand. In adults, infection can be associated with subacute symptoms including fevers and right iliac fossa pain. Abdominal computed tomography usually confirms right iliac fossa inflammation and stool culture reveals typical Gram-negative rod.Aminoglycosides are a first-choice intervention.

stem: A 27-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department complaining of pain in his left arm. He says that the secret service implanted radioactive rods into his arm six weeks ago to control his thoughts. According to his sister, he has become withdrawn over the past year, has not left the house and orders food via the internet. He lost his job 18months earlier, has fitted blackout blinds to the windows in his flat and placed silver foil on the walls. He refuses to talk to anyone, saying that because the track board at the nurses' station is flashing red, the Police are coming. He refuses blood tests but will take tablets. He was reviewed by a psychiatrist in the Emergency Department one week previously who diagnosed him. Which of the following is the most appropriate intervention for this patient's diagnosis?
explanation: This man has features strongly suggestive of acute schizophrenia, with delusions of thought insertion and a primary delusional perception (interpretation of the Emergency Department track board). The fact this patient is compliant with taking oral medication raises the possibility of oral dosing with an atypical antipsychotic such as risperidone or olanzapine, both of which are options under National Institute of Care and Excellence guidelines. Over the longer-term, depot preparations may be considered, particularly where compliance is a problem. Theinvolvement of the multidisciplinary team in managing these patients is essential, with psychological support to induce remission.

stem: A 34-year-old woman who has active relapsing and remitting multiple sclerosis (MS) presents to the General Practitioner for review. She has visual loss affecting the right eye after optic neuritis and ataxia affecting the left side. She is treated with alemtuzumab. Which of the following is the optimal way to monitor for progression of this patient's MS?
options: Magnetic resonance imaging(MRI) brain with contrast
explanation: Although MRI should not be used in isolation to diagnose MS, it can be used for monitoring response to therapy. Consensus suggests a yearly contrast MRl is appropriate to diagnose new lesions with or without active inflammation. Alemtuzumab binds to cluster of differentiation 52, this is a receptor found on mature lymphocytes.

stem: An 82-year-old man is reviewed on the Elderly Care Ward. He is receiving end-of-life care after a massive subarachnoid haemorrhage. His relatives are concerned about increased respiratory secretions and the fact that he is needing regular suctioning by nurses. Which of the following is the most appropriate way to treat the secretions?
explanation: Glycopyrrolate (also known as glycopyrronium) is an anticholinergic agent given subcutaneously in the palliative care setting to reduce respiratory secretions. It is supplied in 200 μg/ml ampules and can be given up to six times per day. It is preferred here to further sedation because it is a reduction in secretions which is the primary objective for intervention. Hyoscine hydrobromide, an alternative anticholinergic is recommended by National Institute for Health and Care Excellence guidelines.

stem: A 39-year-old woman is referred to the Endocrine Clinic because of worsening headaches, episodes of sweating and hypertension which have worsened over the last few months despite starting ramipril 10mg per day. Her blood pressure is 155/90 mmHg, heart rate is 74 bpm and regular. She has a prominent lower jaw and macroglossia. Her body mass index is 23 kg/m. Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin(Hb) 145 g/l 115-155 g/L White cell count (WCC) 7.2×10/L 4-11×10/L Platelets(PLT) 239×10/L 150-400×10/L Sodium(Na+) 143 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/L Potassium (K+) 4.5 mmol/L 3.5-5.0 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 90 μmol/L 50-120 μmol/L Glucose 7.2 mmol/L 7mmol/L Which of the following is the most useful investigation?
options: Glucose tolerance test with growth-hormone measurement
explanation: The constellation of symptoms, signs and biochemistry fit with a diagnosis of acromegaly. The hypertension, dysglycaemia, prominent lower jaw and macroglossia are all pointers to an excess of growth hormone. Growth-hormone secretion is usually inhibited by elevated glucose. In the event that growth-hormone secretion is not inhibited by the glucose load in the oral glucose tolerance test, then the diagnosis of acromegaly is confirmed. A magnetic resonance imaging(MRI) of the pituitary gland is the logical next step to confirm the diagnosis, with surgical excision of the pituitary adenoma the definitive intervention. Somatostatin analogues may be used to improve glucose and blood pressure control before surgery, to reduce operative risk. Acromegaly Media explanations.

stem: A45-year-old woman who has primary biliary cholangitis presents to the Dermatology Clinic with a rapidly enlarging ulcerating lesion affecting her left calf. She says it began as a small pimple a few weeks earlier and has now enlarged with a raised inflammatory border and boggy necrotic base, studded with small abscesses. It is approximately 2 cm in diameter. stem: A 59-year-old farmer who has undergone prosthetic aortic valve replacement some two months earlier presents to the General Practitioner with weight loss, night sweats and intermittent palpitations over the past month. His blood pressure is 132/82 mmHg, heart rate is 72 bpm and regular. He has a prosthetic valve murmur. Splinter haemorrhages are found on examination of his fingernails and Osler's nodes. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin(Hb) 112 g/l 135-175 g/l White cell count (WCC) 12.3×10/L 4-11×10/L Platelets(PLT) 392×10/L 150-400×10/L Sodium(Na+) 143 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/L Potassium (K+) 4.5 mmol/L 3.5-5.0 mmol/L Creatinine (Cr) 122μmol/L 50-120μmol/L Echocardiogram(ECHO) Aortic valve vegitations What organism is the most likely cause of his symptoms?
explanation: This patient's recent prosthetic valve replacement(only two months ago), coupled with symptoms lasting four weeks or more, suggest early endocarditis after surgery. This puts S.epidermidis as the most likely cause due to intra-operative contamination rather than streptococci. Empirical therapy for prosthetic valve endocarditis includes a combination of vancomycin, gentamicin and rifampicin to cover possible staphylococcal infection. Infective Endocarditis explanations.

stem: A 23-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department with pain on passing urine and mucopurulent urethral discharge. He also has a fever and a hot, swollen left knee which he is unable to flex more than 30 degrees and he cannot weight bear. His temperature is 38.2℃. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin (Hb) 143 g/l 135-175 g/L White cell count (WCC) 14.1×10/L 4-11×10/L Platelets (PLT) 291×10/L 150-400×10/L Sodium(Na+) 143 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/L Potassium(K+) 4.5 mmol/L 3.5-5.0 mmol/L Creatinine (Cr) 92 μmol/L 50-120 μmol/L C-reactive protein (CRP) 191 mg/l 10 mg/l Knee aspirate WCC 65000/μl Nucleic-acid amplification test Positive for gonorrhoea Which of the following is the most appropriate intervention?
explanation: This patient has symptoms of gonorrhoea infection which go beyond urethritis alone,including septic arthritis which has occurred as a result of haematogenous spread. Intravenous ceftriaxone is the intervention of choice for disseminated infection; as symptoms improve, there is the possibility to switch therapy to oral cefixime. Screening for other sexually transmitted diseases including chlamydia and human immunodeficiency virus is advised. Gonorrhoea explanations.

stem: A 19-year-old woman is referred to the Renal Clinic with persistent haematuria and mild hearing loss. Her brothers both suffer from progressive renal impairment and hearing loss. Her blood pressure is 129/70 mmHg, heart rate is 72 bpm and regular.Abdomen is soft and non-tender and there are no masses. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin(Hb) 103 g/l 115-155 g/l White cell count(WCC) 8.2×10/L 4-11×10/L Platelets(PLT) 171×10/L 150-400×10/L Sodium(Na+) 141 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/L Potassium (K+) 4.5 mmol/L 3.5-5.0 mmol/L Creatinine (Cr) 117 μmol/L 50-120 μmol/L Urine Blood 1+, protein negative Which of the following is the most likely cause of the patient's haematuria?
explanation: This patient has haematuria with no evidence of renal masses and more severe disease is described in her brothers. This raises the possibility of an X-linked-dominant renal disorder. Alport syndrome(AS) fits with the diagnosis where haematuria and very modest hearing loss may be seen in females, compared with deafness and progressively worsening renal failure in males. AS is caused by defects in type 4 collagen; this is a major structural component of the basement membrane found in the kidney, ear and eye. Angiotensin- converting enzyme inhibitors can reduce progression of proteinuria and renal disease and have an important role to play in treating males with the condition. Alport Syndrome explanations.

stem: A72-year-old man is brought to the Emergency Department after collapsing in the local supermarket. He smokes 20 cigarettes per day and has a chronic cough. According to his wife he has become confused over the past few days. His blood pressure is 145/85 mmHg and his heart rate is 70 bpm and regular.There are coarse crackles and wheeze on auscultation of the chest consistent with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. His body mass index is 22 kg/m. He is mildly confused with a Glasgow Coma Scale score of 13. nvestigations: Which of the following would be the most appropriate pointer towards syndrome of inappropriate secretion of antidiuretic hormone (SIADH) as the underlying diagnosis? Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin (Hb) 123 g/l 135-175 g/l White cell count (WCC) 6.2×10/ 4-11×10/L Platelets(PLT) 164×10/L 150-400×10/L Sodium(Na+) 124 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/l Potassium(K+) 4.5 mmol/L 3.5-5.0 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 92 μmol/L 50-120 μmol/l Chest X-ray Right hilar mass
explanation: Urine sodium of 30 mmol/L is consistent with a diagnosis of syndrome of inappropriate anti-diuretic hormone (SIADH). Levels of urine sodium in SIADH are usually above 20 mmol/l and are often above 40 mmol/L. Paired serum and urine osmolality are below 275 mOsm/kg for serum and urine osmolality is above 100 mOsm/kg. In this case, the hilar mass raises the possibility of an underlying small cell bronchial carcinoma. stem: A 32-year-old woman with known Crohn's disease presents to the General Practitioner complaining of diarrhoea.
